history.heading: Polynesian voyagers
paragraphs: The Cook Islands, 15 islands scattered over a vast area of the South Pacific, were settled by Polynesians around 1000 CE or earlier. According to tradition, voyagers from Rarotonga were among those who sailed to New Zealand to settle it, and Cook Islands Māori are closely related to New Zealand Māori.

Spanish navigators sighted some islands in the 16th century, and Captain James Cook visited in the 1770s; the islands were later named after him. Christian missionaries arrived in the 1820s and converted most of the population.

history.heading: From protectorate to self-government
paragraphs: The islands became a British protectorate in 1888 and were annexed to New Zealand in 1901. In 1965 they became self-governing in free association with New Zealand. Albert Henry was the first premier.

culture.heading: Island culture
paragraphs: Cook Islands Māori and English are official languages. Christianity, especially the Cook Islands Christian Church, is central to community life, with famous a cappella hymn singing.
Drumming and dance are celebrated, and Cook Islands dancers are known throughout the Pacific. Many more Cook Islanders live in New Zealand and Australia than in the islands themselves.

politics.heading: Free association with New Zealand
paragraphs: The Cook Islands are a self-governing parliamentary democracy in free association with New Zealand. Cook Islanders are New Zealand citizens, and New Zealand assists with defence. The Cook Islands conduct their own foreign relations and are recognised as a sovereign actor by many countries, though they are not a UN member.
In 2025 an agreement signed with China without consulting New Zealand strained relations between the two governments.

economy.heading: Tourism and the ocean
paragraphs: Tourism, mainly from New Zealand and Australia, is the largest industry, centred on Rarotonga and Aitutaki's lagoon. Black pearls, fishing and offshore finance also contribute. The country has large deposits of seabed minerals, and deep-sea mining is being explored.
The currency is the New Zealand dollar, with local Cook Islands coins and notes. Emigration has reduced the population.
